newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-World sugar glut seen to cut premiums,shares.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-World sugar glut seen to cut premiums,shares.

text.p: Visions of world sugar wars for market share in a permanently over-supplied market -- with a looming glut in the premium-priced Far East -- jarred the tone of guarded congratulation at the 1997 Australian Sugar Convention, being held here this week.
Australia, having just produced and marketed a record sugar crop, is gearing for further expansion.
C.Czarnikow Sugar Ltd, an export agent for Queensland sugar, has backed this with a view of Australia as top of the world sugar pile.
But the view and the optimism is not fully shared.

Competition between Australia and Thailand, two of the world's most efficient producers, for the Far East market was turning the region into a large surplus area, Patrick du Genestoux, managing director of the Paris-based sugar research organisation Etudes et Recherches Sucrieres (ERSUC) said.
ERSUC sees Far East sugar in large surplus at least to 2000 and sees artificial sweeteners, Brazil and Thailand as all more apt than Australia to take advantage of new market openings.
ERSUC's views were partly backed by other speakers who see Brazil as the emerging sugar force over the next 20 years.
In about ten years, Australia would be producing seven or possibly eight tonnes of sugar, against about five million now, and exporting six to seven million tonnes, du Genestoux said.
"The Far East will then be a surplus area for raw sugar and Australian sugar will be...at a discount no longer...a premium."

Competition between Thailand and Australia would turn the Far East sugar deficit, which now produces a price premium of about US$15 a tonne on raws, for a total annual bonus of $100 million a year, into a "large surplus area", he said.

The Far East sugar market was growing at incredible rates, from consumption of 14.5 million tonnes in 1976 to 39.5 million tonnes in 1996 and on to a projected 52.5 million tonnes in 2006, he said. This had increased its share of world consumption to 33.3 percent in 1996 from 18 percent in 1976.
But production in the region was also increasing, to 38.3 million tonnes in 1996 from 14.8 million tonnes in 1976, and on to a projected 54 million tonnes in 2006, he said.
World sugar consumption was projected to grow healthily at 1.7 percent a year to 2000 from its present 119 million tonnes, then to grow at 1.3 percent a year to 2006.
Production would follow demand growth of about 1.8 million tonnes a year "rather easily", du Genestoux said.
"If food is ever in short supply, it will not be sugar."
There was slack capacity in Europe, central Thailand, China, Argentina and Queensland and huge capacity could be made available by the phasedown of sugar-based motor fuel in Brazil.
Brazil additionally had huge expansion potential, as had southern Africa, India, Thailand, Western Australia and even Queensland, he said.
Production would stay in surplus to consumption for the next few years and reach 129 million tonnes in 2000, he said.
A second-wave sweetener invasion was seen also emerging through importing countries, especially China and perhaps Indonesia, mastering articifial sweetener production.

"If China is not back (buying) something like three million tonnes a year, we project a large permanent surplus to appear (in the Far East) from now to year 2000, particularly if 'Western' invaders, Cuba and Natal, are still selling in the area," he said.
ERSUC sees Far East sugar turning from a 1995 deficit of 100,000 tonnes to a 1997 surplus of 1.3 million tonnes.
Farideh Bromfield of E D & F Man Sugar Ltd said Brazil could emerge as an effective force in the Far East.
By the turn of the century on present trends it would produce more than 18 million tonnes of sugar, with deregulation pushing it to emerge as world number one sugar exporter.

"Given Brazil's potential to...supply nearly 20 percent of world sugar consumption, (it) is likely to emerge as the major force in the world sugar market over the next two decades," said Brent Borrell of Australia's Centre for International Economics.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
